rules.statement: A method that only reads a text input (and does not store it) takes `ReadOnlySpan<char>` instead of `string`, while properties on public request/contract types stay `string`.
rules.why: A `string` converts implicitly to `ReadOnlySpan<char>`, so every existing caller still compiles, and callers can pass a slice without allocating a substring.
rules.check: Look for new or changed helper/utility methods with `string` parameters that are only read, encoded or hashed and never kept. Flag them unless they are properties of a public contract type.

rules.statement: Put a protocol setting that the specification registers per client (such as OIDC client metadata like `id_token_signed_response_alg`) on the client registration model, not on a process-wide `IOptions` configuration class.
rules.why: OIDC registers these settings per client, and the protocol client must not bind process-wide configuration for per-client behavior.
rules.check: Look for new properties on global options classes that correspond to per-client registration metadata in OAuth/OIDC, such as allowed signing algorithms or response algorithms.

rules.statement: Use the existing public constant for a well-known protocol value (for example `AlgorithmCodes.DigitalSignature.None` for the JOSE `none` algorithm) instead of declaring a private constant or a string literal that duplicates it.
rules.why: Duplicated private constants drift from the shared definition that other components already use.
rules.check: Look for new `private const string` fields or inline literals holding algorithm names, claim names or other protocol identifiers that a shared constants class already defines.

rules.statement: When the same hash function is applied to several values of the same output size in a row, allocate the hash output buffer once in the caller and pass it to each call instead of letting each call allocate its own; if that requires a `Span<byte>` inside an async method, move the work into a synchronous helper.
rules.why: Allocating once and reusing the buffer avoids repeated allocations, and dropping this reuse was a performance regression.
rules.check: Look for consecutive hash computations (e.g. `at_hash`, `c_hash`, `s_hash`) where each call allocates or stackallocs its own buffer of the same size, rather than reusing one buffer the caller supplies.
